newsitem.title: USA: Wine giant Gallo cleared in California vintner clash.
newsitem.headline: Wine giant Gallo cleared in California vintner clash.

text.p: A federal jury Friday rejected claims by a California vintner that winemaking giant E. & J. Gallo Winery copied its distinctive autumn leaf bottle to confuse the public and steal sales.

The unanimous seven-member jury in San Francisco cleared Modesto-based E. & J. Gallo of appropriating the so-called "trade dress," or the overall design, of Kendall-Jackson Winery Ltd.'s Vintner's Reserve line of premium wine.
The clash of the California vintners has been the talk of wine business for months.

"This packaging issue has been one of the most critical issues in the wine industry," said Rich Cartiere, editor of California's Wine Business Publications, which has posted daily news reports about the trial on the Internet.
Joseph Gallo, co-president of E. & J. Gallo Winery, said he never doubted he would win the highly-publicized contest. "We never did anything wrong," he said.
Jess Jackson, founder and owner of Sonoma County-based Kendall-Jackson, said the verdict was a "temporary disappointment."

"This is the first salvo," Jackson said, adding that he would ask the judge to set the verdict aside. If successful, he would then ask the court to issue an order blocking Gallo from continuing to use its "Turning Leaf" packaging design.
Kendall-Jackson, a mid-size winery, charged that Gallo was guilty of trademark violations, unfair competition, false advertising and other fraudulent business practices.

Kendall-Jackson claims it has lost $20 million in sales so far because of the way Gallo labels its Turning Leaf brand. The Gallo label is similar to the label on Kendall-Jackson's Vintner's Reserve line.
The Kendall-Jackson wines sell for $10 to $12 per bottle, while Turning Leaf sells for about $7. Both labels incorporate a grape leaf in a wash of autumn colors.

"People buy their product believing it's ours," said Jim Caudill, a spokesman for Kendall-Jackson. He said the confusion has hurt sales as well as Kendall-Jackson's reputation. "It's the same as buying a Chevy and thinking it's a Cadillac."

Friday's jury verdict addressed only part of Kendall-Jackson's charges against E. & J. Gallo. The court has set hearings for next week on the remaining allegations of unfair business practices and false and misleading advertising, a Kendall-Jackson spokesman said.
E. & J. Gallo, the largest winery in the world, has denied any wrongdoing. Gallo began selling its Turning Leaf brand, one of its first premium wines, in September 1995.
